info.name: Travel Platform - C2 (accounts, notifications, payments)
info.description:
Manual test collection for the C2 endpoints: ACC-07a, ACC-08, ACC-09, ACC-11, ACC-12, ACC-14, ACC-16, GEN-01, GEN-11, PAY-01 to PAY-04.

HOW AUTHENTICATION WORKS
The API keeps its token in an httpOnly cookie (ACC-19), and Postman has a cookie jar, so no token is ever copied by hand: run a sign-in request and Postman stores the cookie and sends it automatically on every later request to the same host. Each folder that needs a particular role starts with its own sign-in request, so folders are self-contained.

The jar holds one cookie per name per host, so signing in as the admin replaces the user's cookie. After folder 50, sign in again as the test user before going back to folders 20 to 40.

WHAT YOU NEED FIRST
  cd backend && npm run seed        (reference data: folder 00 asserts 7 currencies)
  cd backend && npm run seed:admin  (the ADMIN account folder 50 needs, ACC-18)
  cd backend && npm run start:dev
Set userEmail/userPassword to an account you register with folder 20 request 01, and adminEmail/adminPassword to the ADMIN_EMAIL and ADMIN_PASSWORD in backend/.env.

WHAT STILL ANSWERS 501
Folders 70 to 90 reach bookings through BookingsPort, which neither the flights nor the hotels module provides yet, so they answer 501 BOOKING_TYPE_UNAVAILABLE. Their tests assert that on purpose; each request says what to change when a booking module lands.

See docs/api/POSTMAN.md for the protocol and the troubleshooting table.

An explicit Cookie header overrides the jar, so this works whether or not you are signed in.

The guard answers the same UNAUTHENTICATED for every failure - no cookie, a bad token, an expired one, an unknown user, a non-active account - so the response never reveals which of those it was.

item.name: 03 A suspended account is refused at once (ACC-16)

request.description:
Run this while signed in, after an admin has suspended your account in folder 50. The guard reloads the user from the database on every request, so the cookie you still hold stops working immediately rather than when the token expires - and the answer is 401 UNAUTHENTICATED, because the guard refuses to identify a non-active account at all.

Logout and the 30-minute idle expiry are ACC-06 and are not built yet.

With a real USER cookie this answers 403 FORBIDDEN, which is RolesGuard doing its job; the role is read from the database on every request, never from the token, so an old cookie cannot claim ADMIN.

This request sends a nonsense cookie instead so it can run without signing out of the admin account, and therefore answers 401. To see the 403, sign in as the test user and delete the Cookie header here.

request.description:
ACC-07a. 200, not 201: nothing is created. The temporary password is shown once and stored only as a hash.

To see the lockout it causes: log in as that account with the temporary password, call GET /api/users/me and get 403 PASSWORD_CHANGE_REQUIRED, then PATCH /api/auth/change-password and watch the rest of the API open up. The old password no longer logs in.

The cookie the account already held keeps working as a token - it is stateless until ACC-06 - but the guard refuses every route except change-password, so the reset takes effect immediately anyway.

item.name: 01 Register and sign in a throwaway account

request.description: Registering logs the account in, so the cookie is in the jar straight away. Use a fresh throwawayEmail: this folder deactivates the account for good.
ACC-12 says 'after confirmation'. The backend does not read an empty DELETE as consent just because a frontend showed a dialog (GEN-13). Try confirm: false and confirm: 'yes' as well.

No row is deleted: the account keeps its data with a deactivatedAt date, so past bookings and payments still point at a real account. Only the status changes, and the blog and itinerary modules derive 'hidden' and 'Deleted user' from it.

If the account had an upcoming confirmed booking this would be 409 UPCOMING_BOOKINGS_EXIST, because a deactivated account cannot sign in to manage or cancel one.

request.description: Testable today.
Testable today. Another account's payment answers the same 404, so payment ids cannot be probed (ACC-11). A malformed id is also 404, not 400.

Testable today, and the single most important thing here to demonstrate: anyone can POST a body claiming a payment succeeded, and it is refused. No cookie is involved - Stripe has none - so the signature is the only authentication, which is why a booking is confirmed from the webhook and never from the browser saying it paid.

A guessed signature is refused with a deliberately vague message, so nothing is learned about the secret. A genuine delivery can only come from Stripe, or locally from the Stripe CLI:

  stripe listen --forward-to localhost:3000/api/payments/webhook
